hints: Picture each chromosome just after DNA replication, with two identical arms joined in the middle. In which early stages are they still joined like this before anything is pulled apart?
Remember the key event of anaphase, when the centromere splits and sister chromatids separate. Which stages happen before this split, and which happen after?
walkthrough:
**Start with what two chromatids means**

Think of the cell cycle first. After S phase, DNA has replicated. So each chromosome now consists of two identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere.

This two-chromatid state is how chromosomes enter mitosis.

**Follow them through prophase and metaphase**

In prophase, chromosomes condense and become visible, but the sisters are still held together. In metaphase, they line up on the equator, still as two chromatids joined at the centromere, with spindle fibres attached.

**Spot when the join breaks**

In anaphase, the centromere divides. Sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles and are now called single-chromatid chromosomes. So in anaphase and telophase, chromosomes have only one chromatid each.

That leaves prophase and metaphase as the two-chromatid stages.

options.A: Not correct. By anaphase the centromeres have split, and in telophase the chromosomes at each pole each have only one chromatid.
options.B: Half right, half wrong. Prophase is correct, but in anaphase the sisters have already separated so there are no two-chromatid chromosomes.
options.C: Correct. In both prophase and metaphase the chromosomes are still made of two sister chromatids held together by the centromere, before separation in anaphase.
options.D: Half right, half wrong. Metaphase is correct, but in telophase separation has already happened so chromosomes have only one chromatid.
